units.title: FPGAs vs Microcontrollers and ASICs
units.tip: FPGAs are programmable chips that can be reconfigured after manufacturing, unlike ASICs which are fixed. They differ from microcontrollers because they run hardware in parallel, not sequential software instructions.

exercises.question: What does FPGA stand for?
exercises.answer: Field Programmable Gate Array
exercises.explain: FPGA is short for Field Programmable Gate Array. Field means it can be programmed after manufacture. Gate Array refers to the grid of programmable logic cells.
choices: Field Programmable Gate Array
Field Parallel Gate Application
Flexible Program Gate Assembly
Fast Processing Generic Architecture

exercises.question: What is the main advantage of an FPGA over an ASIC?
exercises.answer: It can be reprogrammed after manufacture
exercises.explain: FPGAs are reconfigurable in the field. ASICs are hardwired at the factory and cannot be changed, making them cheaper per unit for high volume but inflexible.
choices: It uses less power than ASICs
It runs software faster than ASICs
It can be reprogrammed after manufacture
It is always cheaper than ASICs

exercises.question: How does an FPGA differ from a microcontroller?
exercises.answer: FPGAs run hardware in parallel; microcontrollers run software sequentially
exercises.explain: Microcontrollers fetch and execute instructions one at a time. FPGAs implement logic circuits that run all at once. This makes FPGAs fast for parallel tasks.
choices: FPGAs require no power to operate
FPGAs run hardware in parallel; microcontrollers run software sequentially
FPGAs are always faster for all tasks
Microcontrollers are programmable but FPGAs are not

exercises.question: What is an ASIC?
exercises.answer: An integrated circuit hardwired for a single purpose at manufacture
exercises.explain: ASIC stands for Application Specific Integrated Circuit. Unlike FPGAs, ASICs are designed for one specific task and cannot be reprogrammed.
choices: A microcontroller with parallel processing
An integrated circuit hardwired for a single purpose at manufacture
A type of FPGA that runs software
An acronym for a programming language

exercises.question: Which design path is best when you need many small changes to the logic?
exercises.answer: FPGA, because it is reprogrammable
exercises.explain: FPGAs excel when design iterations are frequent or when deployed systems need updates. ASICs are only worth the effort for high-volume, fixed products.
choices: ASIC, because it runs faster
All three are equally good for changes
FPGA, because it is reprogrammable
Microcontroller, because it is cheaper

exercises.question: What is the key difference between hardware description and software programming?
exercises.answer: Hardware is concurrent; software is sequential
exercises.explain: Software runs one instruction after another. Hardware circuits operate in parallel, all logic gates running at the same time every clock cycle.
choices: Hardware cannot have loops
Hardware is concurrent; software is sequential
Software is only for microcontrollers
Hardware uses more bits than software

exercises.question: Why might you choose an FPGA instead of a microcontroller for signal processing?
exercises.answer: FPGAs process data in parallel at high speed
exercises.explain: Signal processing often needs low latency and high throughput. FPGAs apply the same operations to many data points in parallel, while microcontrollers process them one at a time.
choices: FPGAs process data in parallel at high speed
Microcontrollers cannot handle mathematics
FPGAs require no programming
Microcontrollers have no memory

exercises.question: In FPGA design, what is 'reconfigurability'?
exercises.answer: The ability to reprogram the logic after deployment
exercises.explain: You can update the FPGA's behavior in the field by loading a new configuration bitstream, without replacing the chip. This is a defining trait of FPGAs.
choices: The ability to reprogram the logic after deployment
Running multiple programs at once
Automatically fixing hardware errors
The ability to scale the chip size

exercises.question: What must a hardware description language do that a software language does not?
exercises.answer: Describe concurrent operations and timing explicitly
exercises.explain: HDLs must express what hardware does in parallel and when it happens relative to clock edges. Software languages usually hide concurrency and timing from the programmer.
choices: Avoid using loops and conditionals
Convert English to binary
Use more memory than software
Describe concurrent operations and timing explicitly

exercises.question: Why do FPGA designs often run faster than software for the same task?
exercises.answer: Custom hardware paths eliminate instruction fetching overhead
exercises.explain: FPGAs implement the exact logic path in transistors. Software must fetch, decode, and execute instructions repeatedly, introducing latency and power overhead.
choices: FPGAs use electricity, software does not
Software cannot use multiplication
Custom hardware paths eliminate instruction fetching overhead
Microcontrollers are intentionally slow

units.title: Lookup Tables and Flip-Flops
units.tip: The basic building block of an FPGA is the lookup table, or LUT, which implements combinational logic. Flip-flops store state and synchronize to the clock. Together, LUTs and flip-flops create all logic circuits.

exercises.question: What is a lookup table (LUT) in an FPGA?
exercises.answer: A small memory that implements any boolean function
exercises.explain: A LUT is a small RAM preloaded with the truth table for a logic function. A 4-input LUT can implement any boolean function of 4 inputs.
choices: A table of pin assignments
A timing diagram for the clock
A list of FPGA prices
A small memory that implements any boolean function

exercises.question: How many different boolean functions can a 4-input LUT implement?
exercises.answer: 2 to the power of 16 (65,536)
exercises.explain: A 4-input truth table has 16 rows. Each row's output can be 0 or 1, giving 2^16 unique functions that a 4-input LUT can represent.
choices: 2 to the power of 16 (65,536)

exercises.question: Why is a LUT more flexible than a hardwired AND gate?
exercises.answer: A LUT can be programmed to implement any 4-input logic function
exercises.explain: An AND gate always performs AND. A LUT's contents can be reprogrammed to be AND, OR, XOR, NAND, or any other function, making it universally programmable.
choices: An AND gate uses fewer transistors
A LUT runs at the system clock frequency
A LUT can be programmed to implement any 4-input logic function
A LUT uses less power

exercises.question: What is a 'slice' in FPGA terminology?
exercises.answer: A block containing LUTs, multiplexers, and flip-flops
exercises.explain: A slice is the basic repeating unit in FPGA fabric. It combines multiple LUTs, carry logic, and storage elements (flip-flops) into one configurable tile.
choices: A layer of silicon in the chip
A single lookup table
A block containing LUTs, multiplexers, and flip-flops
A test pattern for verification

exercises.question: In Verilog, which construct maps naturally to a LUT?
exercises.answer: A combinational always block with a case statement
exercises.explain: A case statement that lists all outputs for all inputs is decoded by synthesis as a LUT. The synthesizer fills the LUT's memory with the specified outputs.
choices: A combinational always block with a case statement
always @ (posedge clk)
A for loop with a fixed range
An if statement inside a posedge block

exercises.question: What is a flip-flop in digital logic?
exercises.answer: A 1-bit memory element that stores state synchronously
exercises.explain: A flip-flop is a bistable latch controlled by the clock. It captures and holds data at the rising (or falling) edge of the clock.
choices: A 1-bit memory element that stores state synchronously
A part of a SRAM array
A light switch
An oscillating output

exercises.question: What does a D flip-flop do?
exercises.answer: Captures the value on its D input at the clock edge
exercises.explain: A D (data) flip-flop samples its input on the clock edge and holds that value. On the next clock edge, it samples again.
choices: Captures the value on its D input at the clock edge
Counts from 0 to 7
Delays the signal by one nanosecond
Inverts the signal each clock

exercises.question: Why are flip-flops necessary in FPGA logic?
exercises.answer: To store intermediate values and control timing across clock cycles
exercises.explain: Flip-flops break combinational paths and synchronize data to the clock. Without them, combinational logic propagates changes instantly, making timing analysis impossible.
choices: To store intermediate values and control timing across clock cycles
To amplify weak signals
To reduce power consumption
To implement multiplication

exercises.question: In Verilog, what triggers a flip-flop capture?
exercises.answer: The clock edge specified in the sensitivity list
exercises.explain: always @ (posedge clk) updates on rising edges; always @ (negedge clk) updates on falling edges. The clock edge determines when flip-flops sample their inputs.
choices: A reset signal going low
The clock edge specified in the sensitivity list
Any change in the input signal
An enable signal going high

exercises.question: How many flip-flops are needed to store an 8-bit value?
exercises.explain: Each flip-flop stores one bit. An 8-bit register requires 8 flip-flops, one per bit. This is true in both Verilog and hardware.

units.title: Verilog Modules and Ports
units.tip: In Verilog, a module is a reusable block of hardware with defined inputs and outputs. Ports describe how signals flow in and out. Well-designed modules are hierarchical, hiding complexity.

exercises.question: What is a module in Verilog?
exercises.answer: A reusable block of logic with inputs and outputs
exercises.explain: A module is a container for hardware logic. It defines a set of input ports (to receive signals), output ports (to send signals), and internal logic.
choices: A test bench
A library of predefined functions
A reusable block of logic with inputs and outputs
A behavioral simulation model

exercises.question: What is the purpose of port declarations in Verilog?
exercises.answer: Define the interface signals that connect the module to external logic
exercises.explain: Ports specify what signals enter and leave a module. This interface allows modules to be composed hierarchically into larger designs.
choices: To select the synthesis tool
To specify the module's simulation speed
Define the interface signals that connect the module to external logic
To initialize internal variables

exercises.question: What are the three main port types in Verilog?
exercises.answer: input, output, and inout
exercises.explain: input ports receive data from outside the module. output ports send data out. inout ports are bidirectional (both send and receive).
choices: input, output, and inout
data, control, and status
input, output, and register
read, write, and clock

exercises.question: How do you instantiate a module inside another module?
exercises.answer: List the module name, instance name, and connect ports in parentheses
exercises.explain: Syntax: moduleName instanceName (.portA(signalA), .portB(signalB)). Each instance is a copy of the module's logic, connected to specific signals.
choices: List the module name, instance name, and connect ports in parentheses
Declare a variable of the module's type
Use a new keyword
Import the module file

exercises.question: What is 'port mapping' in Verilog?
exercises.answer: Connecting a module instance's ports to specific signals in the parent module
exercises.explain: Port mapping is how you wire signals. For each input port, you specify which signal it receives. For each output port, you specify where the result goes.
choices: Drawing the circuit on paper
Setting the module's clock frequency
Connecting a module instance's ports to specific signals in the parent module
Writing the module documentation

exercises.question: What is a wire in Verilog?
exercises.answer: A signal that carries combinational logic continuously
exercises.explain: A wire represents a connection between logic gates. Its value updates continuously, following the combinational logic that drives it.
choices: A signal that carries combinational logic continuously
A single bit of storage
An electrical cable
A temporary variable

exercises.question: What is a reg in Verilog?
exercises.answer: A variable type that can be assigned inside procedural blocks
exercises.explain: reg is the data type you assign inside always blocks, initial blocks, or functions. Despite the name, a reg may or may not synthesize to a flip-flop.
choices: Always synthesizes to a flip-flop
A wire that cannot change
A variable type that can be assigned inside procedural blocks
Short for regulation

exercises.question: Can a wire be assigned in an always block?
exercises.answer: No, wires cannot be assigned in always blocks
exercises.explain: Wires are for continuous assignment (assign keyword). Regs are for assignment inside always blocks, initial blocks, or functions.
choices: No, wires cannot be assigned in always blocks
Yes, with any blocking or non-blocking assignment
Only in combinational always blocks
Only with the assign keyword inside the block

exercises.question: What does a continuous assignment (assign statement) do?
exercises.answer: Continuously updates the left-hand side based on the right-hand expression
exercises.explain: assign left = right means the left signal always reflects the combinational result of the right expression. It updates immediately without waiting for a clock.
choices: Continuously updates the left-hand side based on the right-hand expression
Requires a clock edge to apply
Assigns a value once at simulation start
Creates a flip-flop

exercises.question: Which is the correct syntax for a continuous assignment?
exercises.answer: assign wire_out = signal_a & signal_b;
exercises.explain: Continuous assignments use the assign keyword at the module level (not inside always blocks). The right side can be any combinational expression.
choices: always assign wire_out = signal_a & signal_b;
reg wire_out = signal_a & signal_b;
assign wire_out = signal_a & signal_b;
wire_out = signal_a & signal_b;

units.title: Blocking and Non-Blocking Assignment
units.tip: Blocking and non-blocking assignments behave differently in sequential logic. Non-blocking assignments are required for proper synchronous design because they represent simultaneous, parallel register updates on the clock edge.

exercises.question: What is the difference between blocking and non-blocking assignment?
exercises.answer: Blocking updates immediately; non-blocking updates after all expressions are evaluated
exercises.explain: Blocking (=) executes sequentially. Non-blocking (<=) evaluates all right-hand sides first, then updates all left-hand sides simultaneously, matching parallel register updates.
choices: They are identical and interchangeable
Non-blocking is only for wires
Blocking is only legal in testbenches
Blocking updates immediately; non-blocking updates after all expressions are evaluated

exercises.question: When should you use non-blocking assignment?
exercises.answer: For all register assignments inside sequential always blocks
exercises.explain: Non-blocking (<=) is correct for synchronous logic because flip-flops update in parallel on the clock edge, not sequentially.
choices: For all register assignments inside sequential always blocks
When the signal is a wire
Never, it is deprecated
Only for complex expressions

exercises.question: What does a blocking assignment (=) do?
exercises.answer: Executes immediately and the next statement can use its updated value
exercises.explain: Blocking assignment updates the variable right away. The next line sees the new value. This is correct for combinational always blocks.
choices: Prevents the signal from changing
Matches the behavior of flip-flops
Executes immediately and the next statement can use its updated value
Delays the assignment until the next clock

exercises.question: What does a non-blocking assignment (<=) do?
exercises.answer: Evaluates all right-hand sides first, then updates all variables simultaneously
exercises.explain: Non-blocking (<=) is used for sequential logic. All right-hand sides are read based on their values at the start of the clock cycle, then all left-hand sides update together.
choices: Only works for input signals
Is identical to blocking assignment
Evaluates all right-hand sides first, then updates all variables simultaneously
Executes one statement at a time sequentially

exercises.question: Why can mixing blocking and non-blocking assignments cause bugs?
exercises.answer: Results can depend on evaluation order, so simulation may not match hardware
exercises.explain: Blocking updates happen immediately and non-blocking updates are scheduled for later. Mixing them in one block can create race conditions and make simulation disagree with synthesized hardware.
choices: The simulator will run twice as slow
Results can depend on evaluation order, so simulation may not match hardware
It is actually recommended for performance
The synthesis tool will reject the code

exercises.question: What is combinational logic?
exercises.answer: Logic with no memory; outputs depend only on current inputs
exercises.explain: Combinational logic (AND, OR, MUX, adders) produces outputs that are purely functions of the current inputs. There is no state or history.
choices: Logic with no memory; outputs depend only on current inputs
Logic that uses many transistors
Logic controlled by the clock
Logic that always produces a 1

exercises.question: What is sequential logic?
exercises.answer: Logic with memory; outputs depend on current inputs and past history
exercises.explain: Sequential logic uses flip-flops to store state. The output depends on both the current inputs and previous states, creating behavior that changes over time.
choices: Logic with memory; outputs depend on current inputs and past history
Logic controlled by software
Logic that runs in sequence one step per instruction
Logic that only uses AND gates

exercises.question: Which assignment should you use for combinational always blocks?
exercises.answer: Blocking assignment (=)
exercises.explain: Combinational logic has no memory, so blocking assignment is appropriate. The outputs update immediately based on the inputs.
choices: Blocking assignment (=)
Continuous assignment only
Either one, they are the same
Non-blocking assignment (<=)

exercises.question: Which assignment should you use for sequential always blocks?
exercises.answer: Non-blocking assignment (<=)
exercises.explain: Sequential logic uses flip-flops. Non-blocking assignment models the parallel behavior of flip-flops sampling on the clock edge.
choices: Non-blocking assignment (<=)
Either one, they work identically for sequential
Continuous assignment only
Blocking assignment (=)

exercises.question: What does a state machine require?
exercises.answer: Sequential logic with registers to hold the current state
exercises.explain: A state machine needs memory (flip-flops) to store which state it is in. A sequence of states is a classic example of sequential logic.
choices: Continuous assignments
A clock faster than 1 GHz
Sequential logic with registers to hold the current state
Only combinational logic

units.title: Clocks and Resets
units.tip: The clock signal synchronizes all flip-flops in the design, ensuring they update together. Reset signals bring the entire circuit to a known initial state. Both are critical for reliable synchronous design.

exercises.question: What is the role of the clock in synchronous logic?
exercises.answer: To synchronize all flip-flop updates to the same moment
exercises.explain: The clock signal tells all flip-flops when to sample their inputs and update outputs. A single clock ensures deterministic, predictable behavior.
choices: To provide power to the circuit
To reset the design to its initial state
To synchronize all flip-flop updates to the same moment
To determine how much power the circuit uses

exercises.question: What is 'clock frequency'?
exercises.answer: The number of clock cycles per second, measured in Hz
exercises.explain: Clock frequency is how fast the clock oscillates. A 100 MHz clock completes 100 million cycles per second. Higher frequency allows more computations per second.
choices: The number of clock cycles per second, measured in Hz
The duration of one clock cycle
The amount of power the clock consumes
The number of flip-flops in the design

exercises.question: What is a clock cycle?
exercises.answer: One complete oscillation of the clock signal from low to high to low
exercises.explain: A clock cycle is one period of the clock. If the period is 10 nanoseconds, then the frequency is 100 MHz. One cycle equals one period.
choices: A circuit that generates the clock
A single rising edge of the clock
The maximum frequency the design can run
One complete oscillation of the clock signal from low to high to low

exercises.question: What is setup time?
exercises.answer: The minimum time the input must be stable before the clock edge
exercises.explain: Setup time is how long data must be present at a flip-flop's input before the clock edge captures it. Violating setup time can cause wrong data to be captured or metastability.
choices: The duration of the clock pulse
The time to initialize the design
The minimum time the input must be stable before the clock edge
The time after reset when the design is ready

exercises.question: What is hold time?
exercises.answer: The minimum time the input must remain stable after the clock edge
exercises.explain: Hold time is how long data must stay at the flip-flop input after the clock edge. Violating hold time can also cause wrong data to be captured or metastability.
choices: The time between two consecutive clocks
The minimum time the input must remain stable after the clock edge
The duration of the clock pulse
How long to keep the reset signal asserted

exercises.question: Why is a reset signal necessary in FPGA designs?
exercises.answer: To bring all flip-flops to a known initial state at startup
exercises.explain: Flip-flop values can be unknown at startup (shown as X in simulation, and random in a fabricated ASIC). A reset forces all flip-flops to known values so the design behaves predictably.
choices: To prevent overflow errors
To measure power consumption
To bring all flip-flops to a known initial state at startup
To turn off the clock

exercises.question: What is synchronous reset?
exercises.answer: Reset that takes effect on the rising edge of the clock
exercises.explain: A synchronous reset is checked only on the active clock edge, so it takes effect at the next clock edge, matching the sequential behavior of the rest of the design.
choices: Reset that lasts for multiple clock cycles
Reset that happens immediately, regardless of the clock
Reset that takes effect on the rising edge of the clock
Reset that is controlled by a state machine

exercises.question: What is asynchronous reset?
exercises.answer: Reset that takes effect immediately, independent of the clock
exercises.explain: An asynchronous reset does not wait for the clock and clears flip-flops as soon as it is asserted. It is commonly used for power-on initialization.
choices: Reset controlled only by the clock edge
Reset that only works during simulation
Reset that takes effect immediately, independent of the clock
Reset that requires two clock cycles

exercises.question: In Verilog, how do you implement an asynchronous reset in an always block?
exercises.answer: Include negedge reset in the sensitivity list: always @ (posedge clk or negedge reset)
exercises.explain: The sensitivity list specifies what events trigger the block. negedge reset means the block runs when reset goes low, allowing immediate asynchronous reset.
choices: Call a separate reset function
Use if (reset == 0) inside the always block only
Include negedge reset in the sensitivity list: always @ (posedge clk or negedge reset)
Use the assign keyword for reset

exercises.question: Why might asynchronous reset cause problems?
exercises.answer: It can trigger metastability if reset is released near a clock edge
exercises.explain: If the reset signal is deasserted near a clock edge, flip-flops may enter a metastable state, producing unpredictable outputs. Proper reset sequencing prevents this.
choices: It prevents combinational logic from working
It can trigger metastability if reset is released near a clock edge
It stops the clock from running
It always takes two clock cycles

units.title: Synthesis and Simulation
units.tip: Simulation verifies your design behavior in software before hardware deployment. Synthesis converts the Verilog description into actual FPGA configuration. Both are essential for reliable designs.

exercises.question: What is simulation in FPGA design?
exercises.answer: Running the Verilog code in software to verify correct behavior
exercises.explain: Simulation executes your Verilog in a simulator (ModelSim, Vivado, etc.) so you can test behavior before downloading to the FPGA.
choices: Soldering wires to the FPGA board
Running the Verilog code in software to verify correct behavior
Manufacturing the FPGA
Programming the FPGA with bitstream

exercises.question: What is a testbench?
exercises.answer: A Verilog module that instantiates the design and provides stimulus
exercises.explain: A testbench is a Verilog file (not synthesizable) that creates an instance of your design and drives its inputs with test signals, allowing you to observe outputs.
choices: A timing diagram tool
A Verilog module that instantiates the design and provides stimulus
A physical board for testing
Part of the synthesis process

exercises.question: What is behavioral simulation?
exercises.answer: Simulation that treats Verilog as algorithmic code without timing details
exercises.explain: Behavioral simulation executes the Verilog semantically without accurate delay modeling. It is fast for logic verification but ignores timing.
choices: Simulation that treats Verilog as algorithmic code without timing details
Simulation with waveform generation only
Simulation after synthesis
Simulation on a real FPGA board

exercises.question: What is post-synthesis simulation?
exercises.answer: Simulation of the netlist produced by synthesis instead of the original source
exercises.explain: Post-synthesis simulation runs the gate-level netlist that synthesis produced, which checks that synthesis preserved the intended behavior. It can be functional or include estimated delays, and it is slower than behavioral simulation.
choices: Simulation of the design with test patterns only
Simulation of the netlist produced by synthesis instead of the original source
Behavioral simulation with accurate timing
Simulation after programming the FPGA

exercises.question: What is a waveform viewer?
exercises.answer: A tool that displays signals over time as graphical traces
exercises.explain: Waveform viewers (VCD files, GtkWave, etc.) show how signals change during simulation. You can see timing relationships, find bugs, and verify logic behavior.
choices: Part of the FPGA compiler
A test pattern generator
A device that displays the signal on a monitor
A tool that displays signals over time as graphical traces

exercises.question: What is synthesis?
exercises.answer: Converting Verilog code into logic gates and FPGA resources
exercises.explain: Synthesis is the automated translation from high-level Verilog to a netlist of LUTs, flip-flops, and routing. The synthesizer optimizes for area, speed, or power.
choices: Converting Verilog code into logic gates and FPGA resources
Running simulation software
Writing test cases
Programming the FPGA device

exercises.question: What does 'place and route' do?
exercises.answer: Assigns synthesized logic to physical FPGA resources and connects them with routing
exercises.explain: After synthesis, place and route distributes LUTs and flip-flops onto the FPGA grid and determines how to connect them via routing resources.
choices: Generates test vectors
Simulates the design
Assigns synthesized logic to physical FPGA resources and connects them with routing
Verifies the Verilog code

exercises.question: What is a constraint file in FPGA design?
exercises.answer: A file specifying timing requirements, pin assignments, and design constraints
exercises.explain: Constraint files (.xdc, .ucf) tell the synthesizer and place-and-route tool about clock frequencies, pin locations, and area constraints.
choices: A test pattern file
A file that stores simulation results
A file specifying timing requirements, pin assignments, and design constraints
A file that limits the number of lines in Verilog

exercises.question: What is a bitstream?
exercises.answer: The binary file that configures the FPGA's LUTs and routing
exercises.explain: A bitstream is the compiled output of place-and-route. It contains the configuration data that sets up every LUT and connection on the FPGA.
choices: A constraint file
The binary file that configures the FPGA's LUTs and routing
A test file for simulation
The Verilog source code

exercises.question: What does timing analysis verify?
exercises.answer: That all signals arrive in time to meet clock frequency constraints
exercises.explain: Timing analysis calculates signal propagation delays and checks if setup and hold times are met. It ensures the design can run at the specified clock frequency.
choices: That all signals arrive in time to meet clock frequency constraints
That the bitstream file is not corrupted
That the FPGA has enough LUTs
That the Verilog code is syntactically correct
